jsnvu6-e146671-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 2, stating the question to be treated: whether prelacy (positions of rule/authority) and any power of dominion are from God.

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e115.summary: Opens the question: whether prelacy and any power of dominion is from God.

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e123.summary: First objection: what is ordained by God is ordered, per Romans 13; but bad disorder is found in prelacy or authority of dominion (as when a boy rules an old man, or a fool a wise man); therefore such prelacy or dominion is not from God.
claims: Whatever God ordains is thereby ordered (per Romans 13)
Disordered instances of rule (the unwise ruling the wise, the young ruling elders) occur in practice
Therefore not all prelacy or dominion can be from God
concepts: disorder as evidence against divine institution

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e133.summary: Second objection: Hosea 8 says, 'they have rebelled, and not from me,' implying that certain instances of rule or dominion are not from God.
claims: Hosea 8's 'not from me' is cited as scriptural evidence that some rule is not divinely instituted

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e141.summary: Sed contra: among the good angels, and among humans in the state of innocence, nothing would have existed except what was instituted by God; but there is prelacy among the blessed angels, and there would also have been prelacy in the state of innocence; therefore prelacy is from God.
claims: Nothing exists among good angels or unfallen humans except what God institutes
Prelacy exists among the blessed angels and would have existed in the state of innocence
Therefore prelacy is from God

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e154.summary: Second sed contra: Romans 13 states that whoever resists power resists the ordinance of God, which would not hold unless prelacy and dominion were ordained by God.
claims: Scripture (Romans 13) states that resisting power means resisting God's ordinance
This presupposes that prelacy and dominion are themselves ordained by God
concepts: Romans 13 on resisting authority as resisting God

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e165.summary: Opens the responsio by announcing two things to be examined: first, the principal question, whether all prelacy is from God; second, whether prelacy would have existed in the state of innocence, since this is implicated in the argument.
claims: The response requires treating, first, whether all prelacy is from God, and second, whether prelacy would have existed in the state of innocence

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e183.summary: On the first point: prelacy is from divine ordination among humans as to what is due, but not as to its acquisition or bad use—unless, as already said (Distinction 37), sinful acts too are from God in that qualified sense. Proof: what is due to exist among humans according to right reason is due according to divine ordination, since God gave humans reason precisely so they would live by right reason; but according to right reason it is due that there be prelacy among humans; therefore that same thing is due according to divine ordination.
claims: Prelacy as such (what is due) is from divine ordination, though its wrongful acquisition or abuse is not, except as sinful acts generally are attributable to God (per Distinction 37)
What right reason requires is due by divine ordination, since God gave reason to humans for the sake of living by it
Right reason itself requires that prelacy exist among humans
concepts: distinction between the institution of prelacy and its abuse
right reason as expressing divine ordination

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e231.summary: Proves the minor premise of the preceding argument: what is according to right reason in morals is what conforms to the goodness found in natural things, since art imitates nature; but the order of prelacy conforms to the goodness found in natural things; therefore prelacy is according to right reason.
claims: Moral rightness consists in conformity to the goodness found in nature, since art imitates nature
The order of prelacy conforms to natural goodness
Therefore prelacy is required by right reason
concepts: moral order as conformity to natural order

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e245.summary: Proves this by analogy to nature: in natural things, lower things are ruled by higher, the multitude by one—indeed the whole universe is ordered like an army under one leader (per Metaphysics XII). Aristotle (Politics I) likewise says that in every ordered plurality it is natural and expedient that one rule and others be subject; therefore in a plurality of humans it is due and expedient that one preside and the rest be subject—this constituting the order and rationale of prelacy—so prelacy exists among humans by the debt of reason and of divine ordination.
claims: Natural order shows the many ruled by one, and the universe itself ordered like an army under a single leader (per Metaphysics XII)
Aristotle holds that in every ordered plurality it is natural and expedient for one to rule
Therefore prelacy among humans is due by right reason and hence by divine ordination
concepts: Aristotle's Politics on the naturalness of rule
Metaphysics XII's cosmic analogy (universe as an army under one leader)

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e272.summary: Qualifies the preceding conclusion: the attainment and use of prelacy is not always from God—namely when the manner of arriving at prelacy, or the use of prelacy already attained, is evil; this is what Hosea's 'they reigned, and not from me' means. Since judgment about a thing must be made according to how it exists together with all the circumstances whose goodness is required for the thing's goodness, not every instance of prelacy is good or from God, except in the qualified way that evils are from God. This settles the first point of the responsio.
claims: The institution of prelacy as such is from God, but its acquisition and use, when evil, are not (except in the qualified sense that God is the cause of evil acts)
Hosea's 'not from me' refers to the manner or use of attaining rule, not to prelacy as an institution
Not every actual instance of prelacy is good or from God, since goodness requires all the relevant circumstances to be good

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e257.summary: On the second point—whether prelacy would have existed in the state of innocence—answers yes, but not in every mode. The affirmative is clear because where, in a multitude, some are apt to direct and promote others in doing and knowing while others are apt to be directed and promoted, an order of prelacy is fitting; in the state of innocence one person would have been more endowed with the light of wisdom in speculative and practical matters than another, allowing the less-endowed to be directed and promoted toward the good. But prelacy would not have existed in every mode: one person is preferred to another either (1) by referring the one presided over to the ruler's own utility, as a lord over a servant or a tyrant over a subject—which mode would not have existed in innocence, for two reasons: first, because this mode of presiding is licit only with respect to what is ordered to the human as an end, whereas in innocence there was no ordering of human to human (as end), since both nature and grace order the human to God as end, not human to human—though humans would have presided this way over the other animals, using them for their own sake; such prelacy among humans was introduced only after sin, by violence or by man's becoming, through sin, comparable to senseless beasts. Second, because to each is his own good lovable, and it is distressing for one's own good to be entirely subordinated to another's advantage, yet nothing distressing or penal existed in the state of innocence, so neither would this mode of prelacy (as of lord over servant).
claims: Prelacy in the sense of some directing and promoting others toward knowledge and right action would have existed in the state of innocence, grounded in unequal natural endowment of wisdom

Prelacy in the sense of a ruler using a subject for the ruler's own utility (lord over servant, tyrant over subject) would not have existed in innocence, since humans then had no ordering to one another as an end (only to God), and since such subordination is inherently distressing, which innocence excluded
This lord-over-servant mode of prelacy among humans arose only after sin
concepts: prelacy for direction toward the good versus for the ruler's utility
human ordering to God as end, not to fellow humans

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e329.summary: Continues the account of the second mode of presiding: for the good of the one directed, or for the common good, whether directly, or indirectly by removing external impediments (as peoples are defended by kings) or by inflicting penalties for the correction of morals. The first (direct) sub-mode would have existed in the state of innocence, for the reason already given; the second (correction and defense) would not, since before sin nothing could have harmed a human, nor would any will have opposed another's good, so there would have been no need to defend subjects or inflict corrective penalties. It is thus clear that prelacy among humans is due by divine ordination, but its execution by humans is often not from God, except as sins are from God.
claims: Rule aimed directly at the good of the ruled or the common good would have existed in innocence
Rule aimed at defense against harm or corrective punishment would not have existed in innocence, since neither harm nor opposition to the good existed there
Prelacy as an institution is due by divine ordination; its execution by fallen humans is not from God except as sin generally is
concepts: absence of harm and conflict in the state of innocence
final summary distinguishing institution from execution

jsnvu6-e146671-d1e363.summary: Notes that the reply to the arguments on both sides—the two opening objections and the two sed contra arguments—is now clear from what has been said.
claims: The preceding distinctions (between the institution and abuse of prelacy, and between prelacy's modes) resolve all four opening arguments
concepts: summary reply integrating objections and sed contra

jsnvu6-e146671.summary: Question 2 asks whether prelacy and any power of dominion is from God. Objections point to disordered instances of rule and to Hosea's 'not from me' as evidence against a divine source; the sed contra appeals to angelic hierarchy, the state of innocence, and Romans 13 on resisting authority as resisting God. The responsio distinguishes the institution of prelacy from its acquisition or use: prelacy as due by right reason (itself conforming to the natural order in which the many are ruled by one, as in Aristotle's Politics and the cosmic analogy of Metaphysics XII) is from divine ordination, while its evil acquisition or use is not from God except in the qualified sense that sinful acts generally are. On whether prelacy would have existed in the state of innocence, the answer is qualified: prelacy for directing others toward wisdom and the good would have existed, grounded in unequal natural endowment, but prelacy for a ruler's own utility (lord over servant) or for defense and correction would not have, since humans in innocence were ordered only to God as end, not to one another, and nothing distressing, harmful, or corrective existed there. The question closes by noting that these distinctions resolve all four opening arguments.
claims: Prelacy as an institution, required by right reason and conformable to the natural order, is from God, but its wrongful acquisition or abusive use is not, except as sin generally is attributable to God
Prelacy aimed at directing others toward wisdom and the good would have existed even in the state of innocence, grounded in unequal natural endowment

Prelacy exercised for a ruler's own utility, or for defense against harm and correction of wrongdoing, would not have existed in the state of innocence, and the lord-servant mode of rule arose only after sin
concepts: state of innocence and the origin of servile domination
natural hierarchy as ground of political order
